content:
I've pitched a couple people here on the idea of running an autoformalization project in the other direction: turning a formal proof (especially an AI-generated one) into an informal proof that might be easier for a human to understand.

The idea is you still have a blueprint graph, but the documents are "plain english" texts and claude-generated "explainer artifacts".

Instead of nodes turning green as lean signs off, on the proof, you the reader mark them green once you feel you understand them. There is also an optional quiz on each node to check your understanding.

This first example is for one of the recent OpenAI papers, *Generalized Star Height at Most Three*, which has to do with nested Kleene stars in generalized regular expressions.

The informalization is here:


https://tangentproofs.github.io/star-height/
Some light criticism: It is funny to me that there are definitions for both "PlaneMap" and "PlainMap", a PlainMap is a type of PlaneMap :grinning_face_with_smiling_eyes:

Yep. It's just showing whatever was in that lean formalization. The idea is to make it more readable so people actually read it and can suggest ways to make it more understandable.

The format is something I'm continuing to iterate on as I attempt to read it. E.g, since posting, I moved the natural and formal versions side by side and brought the "I understand" check to the top.

Next up is highlighting the definitions a bit better and making sure the different proofs all have a start page with the definitions and final results am in one place.

I agree with the idea. However, I think you should not rely on OpenAI to be able to find the shortest proof, and a shorter proof is always more readable, whatever explainer you later sprinkle in. So, the first step should always be an intensive effort of reduction.

Interesting! Informalization is how our HoTT book started: https://homotopytypetheory.org/book/
It would be great to have good LLM support for that.

I guess there's sort of two audiences here:

  • eventually, it's an explainer for just anybody who wants to understand the thing being talked about.
  • initially, it's an explainer for someone specifically trying to make sense of a particular proof artifact (especially if it's one of these new AI-generated proofs)

Maybe instead of just an "I think I understand this" sign-off, there should also be a way to rate the quality of argument (and request a better one when it's lacking).
